title: Documentary director: there is no typical old age, only specific people
dek: Fan Shiguang, who shot two seasons of Qian Lang, says most marriages end up lukewarm or worse, and growing old together to the very end is rare; what we lack most is not stories, but money, and the habit of seeing old people as specific human beings.
why: The first half is the two hosts in conversation, heavy on feeling; the second half is the director interview, dense with killed story ideas and behind-the-scenes detail, and clearly higher in information density — worth starting at 41 minutes.
who: Listeners following aging, caregiving, family institutions and documentary practice; people in elder care, insurance, legal services and content who can treat the second half, the director interview, as a methodology for choosing subjects.
skip: 0:11-3:53, the opening setup and impressions; you can start straight from the inheritance story at 4:08.

points.h: Five million in inheritance, and the law fighting the deathbed wish
points.body: An elderly woman with no family died in a Shanghai nursing home. While alive she had made a voluntary guardianship notarisation with the notary Li Chengyang, but she never made a will. Sorting through her belongings, the notary found she had left five million in inheritance, including a house, cash and bankbooks. She had said orally, many times, that she wanted to donate it to society and did not want it to go to relatives, but that wish had no legal form. Li Chengyang ultimately chose to follow the law and look for statutory heirs, tracing through archives to children and relatives she had not seen in years. There was disagreement inside the notary office too; some colleagues thought her wish should simply be respected. The compromise was to propose to the inheriting children that 200,000 of the five million go to a fund helping old people with no one to rely on. The children agreed.

points.h: Whether they slept together decides whether the inheritance can be given
points.body: An elderly man with a terminal illness gave voluntary guardianship and his estate to a woman who had cared for him for years and was not a relative — and he had a biological daughter. The notary office argued fiercely over it, and one key point was whether the two slept together: if they did not, the caregiver was merely a nanny or a live-in helper, and an old man leaving his estate to his nanny was morally acceptable; if there was a sexual relationship, the matter stopped conforming to decency. The caregiver was herself married, but had had no contact for years, so in fact the marriage did not exist. So it became a question of an open relationship, and the notary office did not want to bear the risk of offending public morals on the basis of such a judgment.

points.h: Old people finding partners increasingly do not register the marriage
points.body: Li Kangmei, the subject of episode two, was with Lao Li for eighteen years and never registered the marriage from beginning to end, nor was there a de facto marital relationship. The hosts found this far more common than they had imagined: after divorce or the loss of a first marriage, many older people entering a new relationship choose not to marry. They do not necessarily say they love the person; they say they want someone to keep them company, someone to look after them, and behind that is a fairly deep need against loneliness. Lao Li already had a terminal illness, and Li Kangmei's choice was whether to stay to the last moment or to leave early because there was no de facto marital relationship.

points.h: Reality TV forces you to pick a side every five minutes
points.body: The hosts set documentary against reality TV: much of the tension in reality TV is manufactured, backed by a very strong narrative — knowing, for instance, that the audience looks down on mama's boys, so they fabricate a mama's boy on screen. This destroys the audience's tolerance for the complexity of real intimate relationships: every plot beat, every five minutes, demands a position, and that position must be the morally correct one, then gets projected onto some character, and wherever that character goes you take his side. Documentary works the other way: it shows that everyone has it hard, some characters get more screen time and some less, but you can see what each of them is up against, and quite a few of them appear pixelated and anonymous.

points.h: The older generation says I sleep badly, not I'm depressed
points.body: The medical anthropologist Arthur Kleinman found that young people today have a rich psychological vocabulary and can quickly say I'm depressed, I'm anxious, I'm a bit bipolar; but the older generation, even when expressing psychological needs, still use somatised language — I've been sleeping badly lately, I have a bit of a headache — and will not say I sleep badly because I think too much, that I'm a bit depressed. The hosts explain: in our culture it is easier to talk about physical pain, everyone gets a headache or a fever, there is no stigma; once you talk about depression and anxiety, it is a different order of stigma and suffering.

points.h: The idea that got killed: she just wanted to play mahjong
points.body: The director Fan Shiguang told a story he killed himself: the most diligent auntie in a hospice ward, whose husband had bladder cancer and not long to live. She took the bus in at seven or eight every morning and left at five or six in the evening, like going to work, but you could not see love on her face — she just asked the doctors and nurses again and again how much longer other people's family members had. Only later did it emerge that her son had died of a heart attack two years earlier; she was a shidu family, a family that had lost its only child, and her tears had probably run dry two years before. Someone asked what she wanted to do after her husband died, and she said she wanted to play mahjong, because he had never let her play. The first scene shot after the husband died was her finding workers to smash the legs off a two-metre bed with a sledgehammer, one by one, and buying a mahjong table to put in that spot. The story was not used in the end, because the team could not find her real inner world and had only grasped part of the facts.

points.h: Growing old together is rare, not the norm
points.body: Fan Shiguang said the team embedded in fieldwork with roughly fifty families, across the two seasons, and found that going from youth all the way to growing old together to the very end is not the norm, it is rare; most marriages are lukewarm, or even bad. He described the first season's episode Lovers: an old man with Alzheimer's loses control and hits his wife, the daughter forcibly sends him to a specialised nursing home, and the old woman sneaks off to visit every few days, though the hospital will not let her come because it affects his mood. After the old man is sent to hospital, gravely ill, the old woman finally gets her chance to wait on him — cutting his nails, washing his hair, washing his feet. A month or so after he died, she said through tears: my whole life I looked down on him; when we were young I was a good student and he was a poor one, my family were intellectuals and his were workers, he insisted on courting me, and I had no way out, and in the end I muddled through a whole life with him.

points.h: Learning to drive at 95: one sentence strips away the right
points.body: Fan Shiguang said the team worked hard to break stereotypes, because people love to divide into groups and stick on labels — old people are like this, they've gone senile — and there is deep prejudice in that. In the first season there was the story of a 95-year-old man learning to drive and taking the licence test. He caught himself saying, offhand, "driving is all very well, but he is 95 after all", and then asked himself: in that sentence of mine, a 95-year-old has actually been stripped of his rights — that is, he does not deserve them. Public Security Ministry regulations never said a 95-year-old cannot learn to drive, but in that verbal violence the right was stripped away. The bullet comments on the film were full of people saying, can this old man really be allowed on the road, how selfish, what if he hits someone — and all those worries rest on prejudice.

terms.def: An adult with full civil capacity designates a guardian in advance in writing, who takes on the duties if the adult loses capacity.
Expressing psychological distress as physical symptoms, such as using poor sleep or headaches in place of depression and anxiety.
A family whose only child has died, leaving the parents with no children.
Older people whose children are not nearby and who live on their own as a couple, common among highly educated families in big cities.

quotes.text: Whether they slept together — they slept together — why is this detail key? Because if they did not sleep together, this caregiver is merely, say, a nanny to this elderly man with a terminal illness, or a live-in helper, a role like that, and then this old man wanting to leave his estate to the nanny seems acceptable, in terms of moral decency. But if there is a sexual relationship between the old man and the caregiver, all at once the matter becomes not so conforming to decency.
It's as if every plot beat, every five minutes, I need to have a position, and that position is utterly unassailable, it must be the morally correct one.

She will say I've been sleeping badly lately, she will say I have a bit of a headache, but she will not say I sleep badly because I think too much, that I'm a bit depressed, or that I'm excessively anxious.
He said I want to play mahjong. People asked why. He said he never let me play mahjong before.
In fact, from youth all the way to truly growing old together, making it to the very end is not the norm, it is rare — making it to the end. Most marriages are lukewarm, or even bad.
He said that when we were young I was a good student, he was a poor student, my family circumstances were good too, his family were workers, we were an intellectual family.

I asked myself: a 95-year-old, in that sentence of mine, has actually been stripped of his rights — that is, he does not deserve them. Public Security Ministry regulations never said a 95-year-old cannot learn to drive, but in our verbal violence I actually stripped away his rights.
Once you have this label, in fact all these people get gathered up into a prison — you shut them all into a prison, and word after word is a kind of violence.
